title: Frequency-Domain Wiener Filters for Causal Discovery in Dynamic Networks
one_liner: When tracking how things influence each other over time in networks, examining patterns at different frequencies reveals the causal structure far better than looking at raw time values.
lead: Imagine a river system where each station's flow depends on upstream stations from moments ago. To recover which-flows-cause-which, classical methods look at the raw time data and test whether two stations' flows are independent once you account for other stations. But in dynamic systems, a smarter approach watches how patterns repeat at different frequencies, like listening to a song's rhythm rather than each individual raindrop's patter. This paper shows that frequency-domain methods recover network causal structures more accurately and faster than time-domain methods, because frequency splitting reveals hidden causal relationships that time-domain blurs together.

problem.h2: Why time-domain causality fails on dynamic networks
paras: Imagine you want to know: does upstream rainfall cause downstream river flow? A natural first guess is to look at the raw time series — does rainfall pattern A match flow pattern B? But in real networks like river systems, each node (a station) depends on other nodes from earlier moments, not just right now. A naive method (like statistical independence tests on raw values) misses these time-lagged causal links because it is built for static relationships.

The old approach uses Wiener Filters (weighted averages of past values stacked together) in the time domain. It lines up past values with current values and asks how much each past value matters for prediction. But when many things are oscillating at different rates, time-domain Wiener Filters blend all these oscillations into one number, losing the causal signal: a strong influence at one frequency gets buried by noise at another frequency.

callout.html: Look at how the network's influence flows at different frequencies instead of raw time values, using Wiener Filters in the frequency domain. High-frequency wiggles separate from low-frequency trends, revealing which nodes truly cause which.

object.h2: The single thing the paper changes
paras: Wiener Filters are normally applied to raw time-series values. This paper applies them to frequency-domain representations instead: the amplitudes and phases that result from breaking a signal into its repeating patterns at different frequencies.

hidden.name: Phase lag and causality phase signature
paras: When you transform a time signal into frequency representation, every component becomes a complex number: a size (how strong that frequency is) and an angle (how shifted in time that frequency is compared to a reference). That angle is the phase. In the frequency domain, if Node A causes Node B with a one-step delay, that delay shows up as a consistent phase relationship at each frequency: the phase of B lags the phase of A by an amount that corresponds to the time delay. Time-domain Wiener Filters give only a single weight per input; frequency-domain Wiener Filters give a weight for each frequency band, and each weight comes with a phase angle that tells you the exact lag.

The paper measures this phase signature by running Wiener Filters on frequency-domain data (complex numbers with amplitude and phase). The concentration bounds prove that the phase information is stable — slightly noisy data still recovers the same phase relationships, so the causal edges are real.

heat.caption: Hotter cells: frequencies and phase relationships that reveal true causal influence. Time-domain loses this structure.

reads.html: When River A's flow at a certain frequency pattern leads River B's flow by exactly the travel time, we know A causes B. The phase tells us the lag; time-domain methods blur this away.

The Wiener-Phase algorithm estimates frequency-domain Wiener coefficients (complex-valued) and extracts phase relationships. Concentration bounds guarantee that phase estimates converge to true causality.

paras: The root cause: dynamic networks have oscillations at multiple frequencies. A low-frequency trend might mask a high-frequency influence pattern if you only look at raw time data. Time-domain Wiener Filters compute one average weight for how much past-value-X helps predict current-value-Y, because they average across all frequencies in one number. If X's influence is strong only at high frequencies but Y also has high-frequency noise, that single weight gets pulled down — the strong influence is buried in the noise floor, so the method does not see it.

Frequency-domain Wiener Filters split the signal into frequency bands first, so each band is analyzed separately. Then for each band they ask: does past-X at this frequency predict current-Y at this frequency? This isolates each causal influence to its own frequency, so if X causes Y only at mid-frequency, the algorithm sees a strong weight there and zero weights elsewhere, avoiding the averaging problem. Moreover, each frequency-domain weight is a complex number with a phase angle that tells the exact time lag: if the phase angle says 'B lags A by 1 time step' at a certain frequency, and that 1-step lag is the true propagation delay, then the edge is real. Time-domain Wiener Filter weights have no phase — they cannot tell whether a correlation is real influence or just coincidence.

math.h2: The Wiener Filter equation in frequency form
math.words: optimal coefficient for frequency k equals covariance of X and Y at that frequency, divided by variance of X at that frequency
symbols: Wiener coefficient (complex number) for frequency k
how much X and Y patterns align at frequency k

frequency index (0 is DC trend, higher k is faster oscillation)

worked.title: Tiny worked example: a two-frequency river network
lines: Station A has a slow trend (frequency 0) with strength 100, and a mid-frequency wiggle (frequency 5) with strength 40.
Station B depends on A with lags: B's trend mostly ignores A (correlation 30), but B's mid-frequency exactly matches A's mid-frequency delayed (correlation 35).
Wiener at freq 0: W_0 = 30 / 100 = 0.3 (A explains 30 percent of B's trend).
Wiener at freq 5: W_5 = 35 / 40 = 0.875 (A explains 87.5 percent of B's mid-frequency, revealing true causality).
The phase of W_5 is slightly off from zero, meaning B at freq 5 lags A at freq 5 by some time delta — that delta is the network propagation delay, proving causality.

math.note: In frequency domain, strong Wiener weights at high frequencies plus consistent phase lag equal true causal influence; time-domain averages these together and loses them.

items.html: If the time series is too short, high-frequency components are noisy and the Wiener Filter estimates become unreliable at those frequencies. The phase relationship becomes fuzzy.

If a network's properties change over time (e.g., a river channel erodes and flow patterns shift), frequency-domain methods assume the patterns repeat the same way throughout, leading to incorrect phase estimates.
If Node A influences Node B and Node B influences Node A (a cycle), the phase-lag interpretation breaks — there is no single causal direction, and the method will give spurious phase values.

Collect long, stationary time series. Use FFT with sufficient resolution (enough time points to separate low and high frequencies). Verify that recovered causal structure makes physical sense (lags align with propagation delays in the system).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a synthetic dynamic network: three nodes in a chain (A influences B with a 1-step lag, B influences C with a 1-step lag). Generate time series where each node's value is computed from past values of upstream nodes plus noise (for example, B is 0.7 times A from one step ago, plus random noise; C is 0.6 times B from one step ago, plus random noise). Add a low-frequency trend and a mid-frequency oscillation to each node to make the problem realistic. Apply time-domain Wiener Filter and frequency-domain Wiener-Phase algorithm. Measure which causal edges each method recovers.
demo.metric_eq: True edges recovered (percent) = 100 × (correctly identified edges) / (actual edges in network)
demo.closing: Frequency domain should recover both edges at 90 percent plus accuracy, while time domain stays below 70 percent, because frequency domain's phase information separates the time-lagged influences.
